Week 2: Session 3, What Is Underneath the Anger, with care for the wounds the digging may reach.
Week 3: Session 4, The God Who Is Slow to Anger.
Week 4: Session 5, Forgiveness and the Long Release, with a short closing conversation.

bibliography.title: Good and Angry: Redeeming Anger, Irritation, Complaining, and Bitterness
bibliography.author: David Powlison
bibliography.note: Treats anger as a moral response to be redirected, not merely an emotion to manage (2016). The backbone of sessions 1 and 2.

bibliography.title: Anger: Taming a Powerful Emotion
bibliography.author: Gary Chapman
bibliography.note: A practical book distinguishing anger at real wrong from distorted anger at imagined slights. Background for sessions 1 and 3.

bibliography.title: Unpacking Forgiveness
bibliography.author: Chris Brauns
bibliography.note: On the difference between forgiveness and reconciliation (2008). Session 5.

bibliography.title: The Cry of the Soul
bibliography.author: Dan Allender and Tremper Longman III
bibliography.note: On emotions, anger included, as revealing what the heart loves and fears and turning us toward God (1994). Session 3.

bibliography.title: The Wounded Heart
bibliography.author: Dan Allender
bibliography.note: On the buried grief and fear in people who have been harmed. Background for session 3, to be handled with pastoral care alongside local counseling resources.

bibliography.title: Why Does He Do That? Inside the Minds of Angry and Controlling Men
bibliography.author: Lundy Bancroft
bibliography.note: A secular book on patterns of abusive anger (2002), so leaders can recognize harm and distinguish it from ordinary temper. Pair with local domestic violence resources.

bibliography.title: Overcoming Emotions That Destroy
bibliography.author: Chip Ingram and Becca Johnson
bibliography.note: A practical Christian book on destructive anger, accessible background for group members.

bibliography.title: The City of God
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: Book 14 discusses the passions and how they go wrong when our loves are disordered. Session 1.

bibliography.title: Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God
bibliography.author: Jonathan Edwards
bibliography.note: The 1741 sermon on God's anger at sin and the restraint that holds judgment back. Historical background for session 4.

furtherReading: Good and Angry, David Powlison, for the fuller pastoral case behind sessions 1 and 2.
Anger: Taming a Powerful Emotion, Gary Chapman, as a practical companion, read alongside the study's grounding in grace.
Unpacking Forgiveness, Chris Brauns, on the difference between forgiveness and reconciliation.
Why Does He Do That?, Lundy Bancroft, for anyone who needs to understand abusive and controlling anger.
The book of Jonah, read straight through, to let Scripture's most uncomfortable angry man hold up the mirror.

glossary.definition: The idea that anger is a God-given signal that something we love is under threat, to be read and tested rather than indulged or cut out.
Anger provoked by wrong done to others and to God's honor, slow to rise, mixed with grief, and willing to be corrected, like Jesus in the temple.
Anger provoked by wrong done to the self, instant, nursed, quietly enjoyed, and unwilling to be corrected, like Jonah on his hill.
The Hebrew phrase in Exodus 34:6 translated "slow to anger," literally "long of nostrils," a picture of the long breath before the heat.
Fear, unmourned grief, and wounded pride, the things that most often lie beneath a settled anger.
The record of debts we keep and mean to collect, which turns an episode of anger into a way of life.
Releasing your right to make someone pay and handing the collecting of a real, named debt to God. Not denying the wrong, and not the same as reconciliation.
The restoring of a relationship, which takes the offender's repentance and rebuilt trust. You can forgive without reconciling.
Forgiveness as a repeated act, releasing the same debt each time the memory returns.
The truth that someone always bears the cost of a wrong. To forgive is to bear it rather than collect it, as God did at the cross.
A description of anger as often following and masking a more painful feeling such as fear, grief, or shame.
Grief brought openly to God, the biblical alternative to letting sorrow turn into anger.
Real judgment deliberately held back to leave room for repentance. Not indifference, since the same name says he "will by no means clear the guilty."
The old distinction between anger's involuntary rising heat, which isn't itself sin, and the will feeding that heat toward a person, which is the sin of wrath.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Anger usually gets taught one of two ways: as a sin to repent of the moment you feel it, or as a right to indulge. Both are wrong. This five-session study looks at what Scripture actually says: that anger is a signal something you love is under threat, that God himself has it and calls himself slow to it, and that the difference between a fire that warms a house and one that burns it down is the hand that holds it. It covers righteous and self-righteous anger, what lies underneath anger, the God who is slow to anger, and forgiveness as a long release. It says plainly that no one is asked to endure being harmed. Anyone can lead it with no preparation. Come as you are.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We're starting a five-week study on anger. Before anyone assumes it'll just tell you to calm down: it isn't a list of techniques, and it doesn't treat anger as a sin to repent of the second you feel it. It treats anger as Scripture does, a signal that something you love is under threat, the same fire God has and calls himself slow to. It handles the hard things plainly, including that no one is ever asked to endure being harmed. No homework, and no preparation needed to lead a group. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: Most teaching on anger either shames it or excuses it. This one does neither. Five sessions on anger as a signal, on telling Jesus in the temple from Jonah on his hill, on the fear and grief under the heat, on the God who calls himself slow to anger, and on forgiveness as a long release. Come as you are.
quoteCards: Anger is a signal that something you love is under threat. The answer to a touchy alarm isn't to tear it off the wall.
The test of your anger is never whether it feels righteous. It always does. The test is who it's for.
We choose anger over tears because anger feels like power and grief feels like weakness.
Under most long-held anger there's a ledger of debts we mean to collect.
Slow to anger isn't the same as never angry. It's anger held back to keep the door open.
We want a God slow to anger with us and quick to anger with them.
Someone always bears the cost of a wrong. Forgiveness chooses to bear it.
When the memory comes back and you release it again, that isn't the failure of forgiveness. It's what forgiveness looks like.
